# Economics of Markets and Institutions {#economics-institutions}

In January 1914 the Ford Motor Company announced that it would pay many of its
production workers five dollars a day, roughly double the prevailing wage for
comparable work. A hardware store that raises the price of snow shovels the
morning after a blizzard is condemned by its customers, even though the price
rise is exactly what an introductory textbook would prescribe. Apple lets
consumers download most apps without charge but takes a commission from
developers, and payment-card networks reward cardholders while charging
merchants. Governments now sell radio spectrum by auction and create markets in
the right to emit carbon dioxide. None of these practices fits the frictionless
model of a competitive market, in which prices clear markets, every good is
privately owned, information is free, and people care only about their own
consumption.

This chapter assembles the theories that economists developed when they relaxed
those assumptions one at a time: costly bargaining over externalities, shared
goods, incomplete contracts, costly information, unobservable effort,
interdependent demand, private valuations, weak rules, and other-regarding
preferences. Together they form the analytical core of modern industrial
organization, labour economics, law and economics, and market design, and they
supply much of the vocabulary that strategy and marketing scholars use to study
platforms, pricing, and governance (Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-glance)).

```{r tab-econ-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "[Coase theorem](#coase-theorem)", "When do private bargains solve externalities, and what happens when bargaining is costly?", "Dyad / market / policy", "Coase (1960)",
  "[Collective action](#collective-action)", "Why do groups fail to provide goods their members want?", "Group / society", "Olson (1965)",
  "[Property rights theory](#property-rights-theory)", "Who should own assets when contracts are incomplete?", "Dyad / firm", "Grossman & Hart (1986)",
  "[Search theory](#search-theory)", "Why do prices differ for identical goods, and why do jobs and workers fail to meet?", "Individual / market", "Stigler (1961)",
  "[Efficiency wages](#efficiency-wages)", "Why do firms pay more than the market-clearing wage?", "Firm / labour market", "Akerlof (1982), Shapiro & Stiglitz (1984)",
  "[Network effects](#network-effects)", "Why do some markets tip to a single standard?", "Market / industry", "Katz & Shapiro (1985)",
  "[Two-sided markets](#two-sided-markets)", "How should a platform price to two interdependent user groups?", "Platform / market", "Rochet & Tirole (2003)",
  "[Auction theory](#auction-theory)", "How do the rules of a sale shape bidding, revenue, and efficiency?", "Market / mechanism", "Vickrey (1961), Milgrom & Weber (1982)",
  "[New institutional economics](#new-institutional-economics)", "How do the rules of the game shape economic performance?", "Institution / society", "North (1990), Williamson (2000)",
  "[Social preferences](#social-preferences)", "When do people sacrifice money for fairness, and how does that constrain markets?", "Individual / dyad", "Fehr & Schmidt (1999)"
) |>

## Coase Theorem {#coase-theorem}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** If property rights are well defined and transaction costs are
zero, the parties affected by an externality will bargain to the efficient
outcome whatever the initial assignment of rights. Because transaction costs are
rarely zero, the assignment of rights and the design of institutions do matter,
and the real task is to compare the costs of alternative arrangements.

**Origins.** Law and economics. @coase1960, written in reaction to the welfare
economics of @pigou1920. Coase received the 1991 Nobel Memorial Prize in
Economic Sciences, in part for this paper and for @coase1937.

**Level of analysis.** Dyad (polluter and pollutee), market, and public policy.

**Key constructs.** Externality, entitlement (property right), transaction costs,
reciprocal nature of harm, Pigouvian tax, tradable permit.

**Boundary conditions.** The invariance result requires few parties, clearly
defined and enforceable rights, symmetric information, and negligible wealth and
endowment effects.

**Related theories.** [Transaction cost economics](#transaction-cost-economics) (Section \@ref(transaction-cost-economics)),
[Collective action](#collective-action), [Property rights theory](#property-rights-theory),
[Tragedy of the commons](#tragedy-of-the-commons) (Section \@ref(tragedy-of-the-commons)), [Endowment effect](#endowment-effect) (Section \@ref(endowment-effect)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@pigou1920 observed that the private net product of an activity can diverge from
its social net product: a railway's sparks burn neighbouring crops without the
railway paying for the damage. The Pigouvian remedy is a tax equal to the
marginal damage or a liability rule that makes the injurer pay.

@coase1960 challenged this view with a deceptively simple point: harm is
**reciprocal**. If a rancher's cattle trample a farmer's crops, preventing the
damage imposes a cost on the rancher. The question is not how to restrain the
rancher but whether the rancher should be allowed to harm the farmer or the
farmer to harm the rancher. Through examples drawn from English nuisance cases,
Coase showed that if the parties can bargain without cost, they reach the
arrangement that maximizes joint value whoever is initially liable. The legal
rule determines who pays whom, not what is produced. A year earlier he had
proposed selling radio frequencies to the highest bidder [@coase1959], an idea
that became United States policy in 1993 (see [Auction theory](#auction-theory)).

### Core logic and propositions

Let a firm's private benefit from an activity of level $q$ be $B(q)$, and let the
activity impose damage $D(q)$ on a neighbour, with $B$ concave and $D$ convex.
The efficient level $q^{*}$ maximizes joint surplus and satisfies

$$B'(q^{*}) \;=\; D'(q^{*}).$$

The Pigouvian solution imposes a tax $t = D'(q^{*})$ per unit. The Coasean
solution needs no tax. If the firm has the right to operate, the neighbour pays
it to cut back. If the neighbour has the right to be free of harm, the firm buys
permission. Both bargains end at $q^{*}$, and only the distribution of surplus
differs. The theory's propositions are:

- **P1 (Invariance).** With zero transaction costs and well-defined rights, the
  efficient allocation is reached regardless of the initial assignment of rights.
- **P2 (Transaction costs).** As the costs of negotiating and enforcing
  agreements rise, the initial assignment increasingly determines the final
  allocation.
- **P3 (Comparative institutions).** The right response to an externality depends
  on the comparative costs of bargaining, integration, regulation, and taxation.
- **P4 (Markets in rights).** Where rights can be defined, monitored, and traded
  cheaply, a market in rights meets a given target at the lowest total cost.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-instruments) compares the main instruments that
follow from Pigou and Coase.

```{r tab-econ-instruments}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Instrument, ~`What the policymaker fixes`, ~`Information required`, ~`Main strength`, ~`Main weakness`,
  "Pigouvian tax", "Price of the externality", "Marginal damage at the optimum", "Equalizes marginal abatement cost across emitters", "Quantity of emissions is uncertain",
  "Command-and-control standard", "Technology or emission rate per source", "Abatement options at each source", "Simple to monitor and enforce", "Ignores cost differences across sources",
  "Cap-and-trade (tradable permits)", "Total quantity of emissions", "Aggregate target and monitoring", "Least-cost abatement with a known cap", "Price volatility, allocation politics",
  "Liability rule or private bargaining", "Who holds the entitlement", "Courts must assess damages", "No regulator needed when parties are few", "Fails with many parties and high transaction costs"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Policy instruments for externalities.")
```

### Mechanism

Cap-and-trade is the clearest application of Coasean reasoning. A regulator
creates a fixed quantity of emission rights. Firms that can abate cheaply abate
more and sell permits to firms whose abatement is expensive, until marginal
abatement costs are equal across firms, the condition for meeting the cap at
minimum total cost [@montgomery1972]. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-trading)
illustrates the logic for two firms that must jointly abate 100 tonnes.

```{r fig-econ-trading, fig.cap = "Stylised two-firm emissions market. A uniform standard (each firm abates 50 tonnes) leaves marginal abatement costs unequal. Trading moves abatement to the low-cost firm until marginal costs are equal at the permit price, cutting total abatement cost by a quarter in this example.", fig.height = 4.2}
a <- seq(0, 100, by = 0.5)                 # abatement by firm A, firm B abates 100 - a
mac <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(a, mac = 1 * a, firm = "Firm A (low-cost abater)"),
  data.frame(a, mac = 3 * (100 - a), firm = "Firm B (high-cost abater)")
)
cost_uniform <- 0.5 * 1 * 50^2 + 0.5 * 3 * 50^2   # 5000
cost_trade   <- 0.5 * 1 * 75^2 + 0.5 * 3 * 25^2   # 3750
ggplot(mac, aes(a, mac, colour = firm)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("point", x = 75, y = 75, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 76, y = 140, label = "Trading equilibrium:\npermit price = 75", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.3, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 52, y = 230, label = "Uniform standard\n(MAC 50 vs 150)", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Firm A (low-cost abater)" = pal[["blue"]],
                                 "Firm B (high-cost abater)" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 250)) +
  labs(x = "Tonnes abated by Firm A (Firm B abates the remainder of 100)",
       y = "Marginal abatement cost", colour = NULL,
       title = "Permit trading equalizes marginal abatement costs",
       subtitle = sprintf("Total cost: %s under the uniform standard, %s with trading",
                          format(cost_uniform, big.mark = ","), format(cost_trade, big.mark = ",")),
       caption = "Stylised: MAC(A) = abatement, MAC(B) = 3 x abatement. Not empirical data.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

In laboratory bargaining with full information, @hoffman1982 found that pairs
and small groups usually reached the joint-payoff-maximizing agreement whichever
party held the legal right. In the field, @cheung1973 documented that
beekeepers and orchard owners in Washington State routinely contract for
pollination, a textbook example of an uncompensated externality that turned out
to be priced.

Two literatures qualify the theorem. @kahneman1990 showed that people demand
substantially more to give up a good than they would pay to acquire it, so the
initial allocation of an entitlement affects its final allocation even when
trading is costless (see [Endowment effect](#endowment-effect) (Section \@ref(endowment-effect))). @weitzman1974
showed that when abatement costs are uncertain, a tax and a cap are no longer
equivalent: which is better depends on the relative slopes of marginal cost and
marginal damage.

The largest natural experiment is the United States sulphur dioxide allowance
market created by the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, which met its target at
substantially lower cost than a comparable command-and-control approach
[@stavins1998]. Later regulatory and judicial decisions layered source-specific
constraints on top of the cap and drained the market of importance, a cautionary
tale about the political durability of market-based instruments
[@schmalensee2013].

::: {.debate}
**What does the Coase theorem actually say?** Coase himself objected that
economists had read the zero-transaction-cost result as the main message. On his
reading, because transaction costs are positive, rights assignments and
institutions matter, and policy should compare real alternatives rather than
idealized ones. A second debate concerns
**strategic behaviour**: with private information about valuations, bargaining
can break down even between two parties. A third concerns **distribution**:
even when invariance holds, the assignment of rights determines who is richer,
which is why permit allocation is the most contested part of every
cap-and-trade programme.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Carbon markets.** The European Union Emissions Trading System, launched in
2005, caps emissions from power generation and heavy industry and allows covered
installations to trade allowances. Its first phase illustrated the importance of
accurate rights definition: allowances were allocated largely free on the basis
of estimated needs, and when verified emissions data showed that the market was
over-allocated, prices collapsed to near zero by 2007 because first-phase
allowances could not be carried into the next phase. Later reforms moved toward
auctioning and introduced a Market Stability Reserve that withdraws surplus
allowances. For firms, the managerial implications follow directly from
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-trading): treat carbon as a priced input, abate
wherever internal abatement is cheaper than the allowance price, and buy
allowances where it is not. Many firms also apply an internal carbon price to
investment appraisal.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Bilateral disputes over externalities are more likely to be resolved by
  private agreement when the number of affected parties is small and property
  rights are clearly documented.
- *H2.* Under a cap-and-trade programme, dispersion of marginal abatement cost
  across covered firms declines as market liquidity rises.

**Designs.** Laboratory bargaining experiments varying rights assignment and
information. Difference-in-differences around the introduction or reform of
permit markets. Event studies of allowance price shocks on covered firms'
stock returns.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Reading Coase as an argument against all regulation.** The theorem does not say
that externalities take care of themselves. It says they would if transaction
costs were zero, which they rarely are. When the affected parties number in the
millions (as with air pollution or carbon dioxide), private bargaining is
impossible, and the relevant comparison is among imperfect institutions: taxes,
caps, standards, and liability. Citing Coase to oppose a carbon market inverts
the theorem: tradable permits are themselves a Coasean creation of property
rights.
:::

## Collective Action {#collective-action}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Rational, self-interested members of a large group will not
contribute voluntarily to a good that benefits the whole group, because each
receives the benefit whether or not he or she contributes. Large groups therefore
organize only when they can offer **selective incentives** or impose coercion.

**Origins.** Public economics and political economy. @samuelson1954 formalized
public goods. @olson1965 extended the logic to groups, unions, cartels, and
lobbies.

**Level of analysis.** Group, organization, industry, and society.

**Key constructs.** Public good (non-rival and non-excludable), free riding,
group size, selective incentives, privileged and latent groups, conditional
cooperation, peer punishment.

**Boundary conditions.** Benefits cannot be withheld from non-contributors,
contributions are costly, and members interact anonymously. Repeated
interaction and sanctioning weaken the prediction.

**Related theories.** [Tragedy of the commons](#tragedy-of-the-commons) (Section \@ref(tragedy-of-the-commons)),
[Social loafing](#social-loafing) (Section \@ref(social-loafing)), [Social preferences](#social-preferences),
[Social norms](#social-norms) (Section \@ref(social-norms)), [New institutional economics](#new-institutional-economics).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@samuelson1954 defined a collective consumption good as one whose consumption by
one person does not reduce the amount available to anyone else. He showed that
efficient provision requires the *sum* of individuals' marginal rates of
substitution between the public good $G$ and a private good to equal the
marginal rate of transformation:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} MRS_{i}^{G,x} \;=\; MRT^{G,x}.$$

Because people can free ride, decentralized markets underprovide public goods.

@olson1965 showed that shared interests do not imply collective action. Every
member of a trade association benefits from favourable legislation, but each
firm's contribution barely affects the outcome and the firm benefits whether or
not it pays. The argument explains why small, concentrated interests often
defeat large, diffuse ones, and why unions and professional associations bundle
political activity with private benefits for members. The closely related
[Tragedy of the commons](#tragedy-of-the-commons) (Section \@ref(tragedy-of-the-commons)) concerns resources that are
rival in consumption, and @ostrom1990's work on self-governing communities,
discussed there, is the most influential response to both problems.

### Core logic and propositions

The **linear public goods game** captures the structure. Each of $n$ players
receives an endowment $e$ and chooses a contribution $c_i$ to a group project.
Contributions are multiplied and shared equally:

$$\pi_i \;=\; e - c_i + m \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j, \qquad \frac{1}{n} < m < 1.$$

Each unit contributed returns only $m < 1$ to the contributor, so contributing
nothing is a dominant strategy. Each unit contributed returns $nm > 1$ to the
group, so full contribution is socially efficient. The gap between the two is
the collective action problem. Olson's propositions follow:

- **P1 (Group size).** Larger groups are less likely to provide collective goods,
  because each member's share of the benefit is smaller, each contribution is less
  noticeable, and organizing costs are higher.
- **P2 (Selective incentives).** Large ("latent") groups mobilize when
  participation is tied to private benefits available only to contributors, such
  as insurance, journals, training, or certification.
- **P3 (Privileged groups).** If one member values the good more than its full
  cost, the good is provided, and the large member bears a disproportionate share
  (Olson's "exploitation of the great by the small").
- **P4 (Sanctions and reciprocity).** Contributions are sustained when members can
  observe one another and punish free riders, an extension developed in
  experimental work [@fehr2000a].

### Mechanism

In repeated public goods experiments, contributions typically start well above
zero and decline as cooperative participants discover that others free ride. Many
participants are **conditional cooperators** who contribute more when they
believe others are contributing [@fischbacher2001]. @fehr2000a showed that
allowing participants to pay to punish low contributors reverses the decline.
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-pgg) sketches the qualitative pattern.

```{r fig-econ-pgg, fig.cap = "Stylised pattern of contributions in a repeated public goods game with and without peer punishment. Without punishment, contributions decay toward free riding. With costly punishment, contributions are sustained. Qualitative pattern consistent with Fehr and Gachter (2000a). Illustrative, not their data.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1965)
periods <- 1:10
pgg <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(period = periods,
             share = pmax(0.05, 0.48 * exp(-0.17 * (periods - 1)) + rnorm(10, 0, 0.015)),
             condition = "No punishment"),
  data.frame(period = periods,
             share = pmin(0.95, 0.55 + 0.035 * (periods - 1) + rnorm(10, 0, 0.015)),
             condition = "With peer punishment")
)
ggplot(pgg, aes(period, share, colour = condition)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("No punishment" = pal[["orange"]], "With peer punishment" = pal[["blue"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = periods) +
  labs(x = "Period", y = "Average contribution (share of endowment)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Free riding erodes cooperation unless it can be punished",
       caption = "Illustrative simulation of a qualitative pattern. Not experimental data.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The free-rider prediction is confirmed in its direction but not in its
magnitude: people contribute more than pure self-interest predicts, especially
early, and their behaviour depends on what they expect others to do. Cultural
context matters. @herrmann2008 ran the same public goods game with punishment in
16 subject pools around the world and found that in some societies punished
participants frequently retaliated against high contributors (**antisocial
punishment**), which undermined cooperation. @ostrom2000 reviews field and
laboratory evidence that communities develop norms and graduated sanctions that
sustain collective action well beyond what Olson's model implies.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-ca-solutions) summarizes the main solutions identified
across this literature.

```{r tab-econ-ca-solutions}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Solution, ~Logic, ~`Business or policy example`,
  "Selective incentives", "Bundle the public good with private benefits for contributors", "Trade association membership that includes data, events, and certification",
  "Coercion or mandate", "Make contribution compulsory", "Taxes, compulsory levies for generic product advertising",
  "Privileged sponsor", "A member large enough to gain from providing the good alone", "A dominant firm funding an open industry standard",
  "Federated structure", "Organize small groups in which contributions are noticeable", "Local chapters of national associations",
  "Monitoring and sanctions", "Make free riding visible and costly", "Peer review of contributions in research consortia",
  "Norms and reputation", "Social approval for contributors, disapproval for free riders", "Public recognition of open-source maintainers"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Solutions to collective action problems.")
```

::: {.debate}
**Is group size really the enemy of cooperation?** If the good is purely
non-rival, a larger group may include more members with high valuations, so the
probability that someone provides it can rise with size, and field research on
commons governance finds no simple monotonic effect [@ostrom2000]. A second
critique targets the behavioural assumption: conditional cooperators and willing
punishers mean that institutions which make contributions visible can unlock
cooperation that Olson's model rules out [@fehr2000a; @fischbacher2001]. A third
notes that large-scale successes such as open-source software rely on selective
incentives Olson anticipated: reputation, learning, and career signalling.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Underfunded digital infrastructure.** Open-source software is a public good
for the firms that build on it. In April 2014 the Heartbleed vulnerability in
OpenSSL, a widely used cryptographic library, revealed that critical code relied
on a very small group of mostly volunteer maintainers, although many large firms
depended on it. The response followed Olson's playbook: the Linux Foundation
organized the Core Infrastructure Initiative, through which large technology
firms (a privileged group) jointly funded critical projects, with public
recognition of sponsors as a selective incentive.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Contributions to an inter-firm consortium will be higher when contributions
  are publicly disclosed to other members.
- *H2.* The positive effect of membership benefits on association membership will
  be stronger in industries with many small firms than in concentrated industries.

**Designs.** Laboratory and online public goods games. Field experiments that
vary the visibility of contributions (for example, charitable giving). Panel
data on association membership and lobbying expenditure.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Calling every shared good a public good.** Many "collective" goods are
excludable: industry data, certification, and standards can be restricted to
members. Such club goods face weaker free-rider problems, and the right remedy is
pricing access, not subsidy or mandate.
:::

## Property Rights Theory {#property-rights-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** When contracts are incomplete, ownership of physical assets
confers **residual control rights**, the right to decide how assets are used in
circumstances the contract does not cover. Ownership therefore shapes each
party's bargaining position after investments are sunk, and hence each party's
incentive to invest beforehand. Assets should be owned by the party whose
investment matters most.

**Origins.** Economics of the firm. @grossman1986, @hart1990, synthesized in
@hart1995. Hart shared the 2016 Nobel Memorial Prize for contract theory.

**Level of analysis.** Dyad (buyer and supplier) and the boundary of the firm.

**Key constructs.** Incomplete contracts, residual control rights,
relationship-specific investment, hold-up, outside option, asset
complementarity, indispensability.

**Boundary conditions.** Some investments cannot be specified in an enforceable
contract, parties can renegotiate after uncertainty resolves, and ownership of
physical (or legally protectable) assets affects outside options.

**Related theories.** [Transaction cost economics](#transaction-cost-economics) (Section \@ref(transaction-cost-economics)),
[Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)), [Coase theorem](#coase-theorem),
[Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@coase1937 asked why some transactions are organized inside firms rather than
across markets. Williamson's [Transaction cost economics](#transaction-cost-economics) (Section \@ref(transaction-cost-economics))
and @klein1978 answered that relationship-specific investments create
appropriable quasi-rents that a trading partner can try to capture by
threatening to walk away, the **hold-up** problem, and that vertical integration
suppresses this opportunism. @grossman1986 accepted the hold-up premise but
asked why, if integration cures opportunism, firms do not integrate everything.
Their answer was that integration does not remove incentive problems. It moves
them. When firm 1 buys firm 2, the former owner-manager of firm 2 becomes an
employee with weaker incentives, because the assets she needs to capture the
returns on her effort are now controlled by someone else. The crucial step was
to define **ownership as the residual right** to decide everything the contract
leaves unspecified. With complete contracts, ownership would not matter. With
incomplete contracts, it determines who has the upper hand when the unexpected
happens.

### Core logic and propositions

Consider two parties who each make a non-contractible investment $i_k$ before
they trade. Trade generates joint value $v(i_1, i_2)$. If bargaining breaks down,
each party receives an outside option $o_k^{g}(i_k)$ that depends on which assets
it controls under ownership structure $g$ (non-integration, party 1 owns, party 2
owns). With symmetric Nash bargaining, party 1's payoff is

$$u_1 \;=\; o_1^{g} + \tfrac{1}{2}\left[v(i_1, i_2) - o_1^{g} - o_2^{g}\right] - i_1,$$

so party 1's marginal return on investment is
$\tfrac{1}{2}\,\partial v/\partial i_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\partial o_1^{g}/\partial i_1$.
Because the party captures only part of the value its investment creates,
investment falls short of the first best. Owning more assets increases
$\partial o_1^{g}/\partial i_1$ and therefore increases party 1's investment, but
at the expense of party 2's. @hart1990 and @hart1995 derive the following
propositions:

- **P1 (Importance of investment).** Ownership should go to the party whose
  non-contractible investment contributes more to joint value.
- **P2 (Independent assets).** Assets that are economically independent should be
  owned separately.
- **P3 (Complementary assets).** Assets that are strictly complementary should be
  owned together.
- **P4 (Indispensability).** A party whose human capital is indispensable to an
  asset should own that asset.
- **P5 (Costs of integration).** Integration raises the investment incentives of
  the acquirer and lowers those of the acquired party. It is efficient only when
  the first effect dominates.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-prt) summarizes the mechanism.

```{r fig-econ-prt, fig.cap = "Mechanism of property rights theory: with incomplete contracts, ownership allocates residual control rights, which shape outside options and bargaining power ex post, and therefore investment incentives ex ante."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  C [label = "Incomplete\\ncontract", %s]
  O [label = "Ownership of\\nphysical assets", %s]
  R [label = "Residual control\\nrights", %s]
  B [label = "Outside options and\\nex post bargaining power", %s]
  I [label = "Ex ante specific\\ninvestment", %s]
  V [label = "Joint surplus", %s]
  S [label = "Asset complementarity\\nand specificity", %s]
  C -> R
  O -> R -> B -> I -> V
  S -> B [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

Clean tests are difficult because investments are, by assumption, hard to
observe. @baker2003 provide one of the best: the diffusion of on-board computers
in United States trucking changed what could be monitored and contracted, which
in turn changed who owned the trucks. The most famous historical case is
contested. @klein1978 described General Motors' 1926 acquisition of Fisher Body
as a response to hold-up by a supplier that had refused to locate plants near
GM's, but later archival work disputed that account [@coase2000; @freeland2000;
@casadesus2000], a reminder that canonical examples deserve primary-source
scrutiny.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-prt-tce) contrasts property rights theory with
[Transaction cost economics](#transaction-cost-economics) (Section \@ref(transaction-cost-economics)), its closest relative.

```{r tab-econ-prt-tce}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Transaction cost economics`, ~`Property rights theory`,
  "Key source", "Williamson (1975, 1985)", "Grossman & Hart (1986), Hart & Moore (1990)",
  "Unit of analysis", "The transaction", "Ownership of assets",
  "Main inefficiency", "Ex post haggling and maladaptation", "Ex ante underinvestment",
  "Role of integration", "Replaces haggling with authority (fiat)", "Reallocates residual control rights",
  "Cost of integration", "Bureaucratic costs, weaker incentives", "Lower investment incentives for the acquired party",
  "Prediction", "Integrate when asset specificity and uncertainty are high", "Give ownership to the party whose investment matters most",
  "Typical evidence", "Make-or-buy regressions on asset specificity", "Ownership changes after shifts in contractibility"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Transaction cost economics and property rights theory compared.")
```

::: {.debate}
**How firm are the foundations?** @maskin1999 argued that if parties can foresee
the payoffs of future contingencies, even without describing them, clever
mechanisms can in principle restore efficient investment, undermining the
incomplete-contracts premise. Defenders reply that such mechanisms are fragile
and rarely observed. A second critique is empirical: because the two theories
in Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-prt-tce) often predict the same make-or-buy choice,
findings that asset specificity predicts integration cannot distinguish them.
Discriminating tests need settings where the theories diverge.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: who should own the tooling?** An automotive
manufacturer asks a supplier to build specialized moulds for a new component.
If the supplier owns the moulds, it has a strong incentive to maintain and
improve them, but the manufacturer fears hold-up once switching is costly. If
the manufacturer owns the moulds, it can move them if the relationship sours,
which disciplines the supplier but weakens its incentive to improve the process.
Property rights theory predicts manufacturer ownership when the manufacturer's
investments matter more than the supplier's improvement effort.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Following a technology that makes a supplier's effort contractible, the
  probability that the buyer owns the relevant asset will rise.
- *H2.* In R&D alliances, the partner whose non-contractible know-how is more
  important to the project is more likely to hold the resulting intellectual
  property.

**Designs.** Natural experiments in contractibility (new monitoring technologies,
legal changes). Contract-level data on ownership and control clauses. Panel
studies of inventors before and after acquisitions.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating integration as free.** A common misuse is to cite hold-up as a reason
to integrate without asking whose incentives integration destroys. Ownership is
a zero-sum allocation of control: strengthening one party's investment
incentives weakens another's. Ignoring this trade-off leads to systematic
over-integration.
:::

## Search Theory {#search-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** When information about prices, products, or trading partners is
costly to acquire, buyers and job seekers search only until the expected gain
from one more search falls to its cost. Price dispersion for identical goods and
the coexistence of unemployment and vacancies are therefore equilibrium
outcomes, not anomalies.

**Origins.** Economics of information. @stigler1961, @mccall1970,
@diamond1971, and for labour markets @mortensen1994. Diamond, Mortensen, and
Pissarides shared the 2010 Nobel Memorial Prize.

**Level of analysis.** Individual searcher, firm, and market.

**Key constructs.** Search cost, price dispersion, reservation price and
reservation wage, sequential versus fixed-sample search, matching function,
market tightness.

**Boundary conditions.** Offers vary across sellers or employers, finding them
is costly. Free, universally used comparison tools shrink its predictions.

**Related theories.** [Information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry)),
[Bounded rationality](#bounded-rationality) (Section \@ref(bounded-rationality)), [Two-sided markets](#two-sided-markets),
[Reference price](#reference-price) (Section \@ref(reference-price)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@stigler1961 [p. 213] observed that information occupies "a slum dwelling in the
town of economics": price theory had assumed away the problem of finding out
what prices are. Because ignorance is costly to remove, rational buyers stop
searching before they find the lowest price, and sellers can sustain different
prices for identical goods. The more a buyer spends, the more search pays.

@mccall1970 modelled **sequential** search for jobs, in
which a worker samples one offer at a time and stops at the first offer above a
**reservation wage**. @diamond1971 showed a startling equilibrium implication:
if all consumers face even a tiny positive search cost and firms set prices,
the unique equilibrium is for every firm to charge the monopoly price, because
no consumer will search to find a slightly lower one (the **Diamond paradox**).
Later work restored price dispersion as an equilibrium by allowing consumers to
differ in search costs or in how many quotes they obtain [@varian1980;
@burdett1983]. In labour economics, @mortensen1994 built a model of job creation
and destruction in which a **matching function** links unemployed workers and
vacancies, explaining why both exist at once and how they move over the business
cycle.

### Core logic and propositions

In sequential search with cost $c$ per offer and wage offers drawn from
distribution $F$, the optimal policy is to accept the first offer at or above a
reservation wage $w^{R}$ that equates the cost of one more draw with its expected
gain:

$$c \;=\; \int_{w^{R}}^{\infty} \left(w - w^{R}\right)\, dF(w).$$

Higher search costs lower the reservation wage, and a more dispersed offer
distribution raises it. In matching models, hires $m(u, v)$ increase in
unemployment $u$ and vacancies $v$, and **market tightness** $\theta = v/u$
governs how fast workers find jobs and firms fill vacancies. The propositions
are:

- **P1 (Optimal stopping).** Searchers stop when the marginal gain of search
  equals its cost, so they rationally accept prices above the minimum.
- **P2 (Stakes).** Search effort and price convergence increase with the size of
  the expenditure [@stigler1961].
- **P3 (Search costs and market power).** Higher search costs raise equilibrium
  prices. With homogeneous positive search costs, prices rise to the monopoly
  level [@diamond1971].
- **P4 (Frictional unemployment).** Unemployment and vacancies coexist, and lower
  search frictions raise matching efficiency [@mortensen1994].

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-search) illustrates Stigler's fixed-sample logic: each
additional quote lowers the expected minimum price by less and less, so a
business buying ten units rationally collects many more quotes than a household
buying one.

```{r fig-econ-search, fig.cap = "Stylised Stigler search model. Prices are uniform between 80 and 120 and each quote costs 2. The expected saving from the k-th quote falls quickly, so a buyer of one unit stops at about four quotes while a buyer of ten units collects about thirteen.", fig.height = 4}
k <- 2:16
spread <- 40                                   # price range: 80 to 120
gain <- spread / (k * (k + 1))                 # E[min of k-1] - E[min of k] for uniform prices
search <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(k, gain = 1 * gain, buyer = "Household buying 1 unit"),
  data.frame(k, gain = 10 * gain, buyer = "Business buying 10 units")
)
quote_cost <- 2
stop_at <- search |> group_by(buyer) |> filter(gain >= quote_cost) |> summarise(k = max(k))
ggplot(search, aes(k, gain, colour = buyer)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = quote_cost, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(data = stop_at, aes(xintercept = k, colour = buyer), linetype = "dotted", show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = quote_cost + 1.5, label = "Cost of one more quote", hjust = 1,
           size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Household buying 1 unit" = pal[["orange"]],
                                 "Business buying 10 units" = pal[["blue"]])) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 16, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Number of price quotes collected (k)", y = "Expected saving from the k-th quote (log scale)",
       colour = NULL, title = "Search pays more when more is at stake",
       caption = "Stylised: expected saving = units x 40 / (k(k + 1)). Dotted lines mark optimal stopping.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The internet was expected to collapse price dispersion. @brynjolfsson2000 found
that online prices for books and CDs were lower than offline prices but that
online dispersion remained substantial. @brown2002 found that the growth of
comparison sites for term life insurance was associated with meaningful price
reductions. @ellison2009 showed that retailers on a price comparison site
responded to highly price-elastic search by **obfuscation**: advertising a
low-quality product at a low price and steering buyers to higher-margin
upgrades. Search costs are partly chosen by sellers. In labour economics,
@shimer2005 showed that the standard matching model with plausible parameters
generates far smaller fluctuations in unemployment and vacancies than observed,
prompting a large literature on wage rigidity.

```{r tab-econ-search}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Market, ~`Source of search cost`, ~`Observable consequence`, ~`Managerial lever`,
  "Consumer retail", "Time to visit stores or compare sites", "Persistent price dispersion", "Price-match guarantees, comparison listings",
  "Insurance and finance", "Complex products, hard to compare", "Dispersion in premiums and fees", "Standardized disclosures, aggregators",
  "Labour", "Finding and screening candidates", "Unemployment and vacancies coexist", "Referral programmes, job platforms",
  "Housing", "Viewing, negotiating, coordinating", "Long time-to-sale, agent intermediation", "Listing platforms, virtual tours",
  "B2B procurement", "Qualifying suppliers, requesting quotes", "Sticky supplier relationships", "Reverse auctions, supplier portals"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Search frictions across markets.")
```

::: {.debate}
**Do lower search costs always help consumers?** Comparison tools should
intensify competition, but firms respond by obfuscating, adding fees revealed
late in the purchase, or differentiating products so that they are harder to
compare [@ellison2009]. Lower search costs can also benefit sellers by improving
matches. The welfare effect of a search technology therefore depends on how
sellers adapt.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Comparison sites and obfuscation.** Price comparison platforms for insurance,
flights, and consumer electronics lower search costs for consumers and push
sellers toward the lowest headline price. Sellers have responded with
partitioned prices, add-on fees, and stripped-down base products, a pattern
consistent with @ellison2009. For managers, the headline price is only one
dimension of search: firms can compete by being easy to compare or by making
comparison harder (Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-search) lists levers in other
markets). For regulators, disclosure rules on total price can be more effective
than measures that only make search cheaper.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Price dispersion for an identical product will be lower in categories
  with higher average expenditure per purchase.
- *H2.* Entry of a comparison platform into a market will reduce average prices
  and increase the use of add-on fees.

**Designs.** Web-scraped price panels, clickstream data on consumer search,
field experiments that vary search costs, structural estimation of search
models.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Calling price dispersion irrational.** Paying more than the lowest available
price is not evidence that consumers are irrational. It is exactly what
optimal search predicts when search is costly. Before attributing dispersion to
bias, measure search costs and the stakes of the purchase.
:::

## Efficiency Wages {#efficiency-wages}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Firms may rationally pay more than the market-clearing wage
because higher pay raises productivity: it elicits reciprocal effort, makes
shirking costlier, reduces turnover, and attracts better applicants. Because
firms do not cut wages even when job seekers are queuing, involuntary
unemployment can persist in equilibrium.

**Origins.** Labour economics and macroeconomics. @akerlof1982 (gift exchange),
@shapiro1984 (shirking), with historical evidence from @raff1987. The
cost-minimizing condition goes back to @solow1979.

**Level of analysis.** Firm and labour market.

**Key constructs.** Wage premium, effort, monitoring intensity, detection
probability, unemployment as a discipline device, gift exchange, reference
(fair) wage, turnover cost.

**Boundary conditions.** Effort is imperfectly observable or contractible,
turnover is costly, and workers compare pay with a reference. Where piece rates
are feasible, efficiency wage motives weaken.

**Related theories.** [Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)), [Social preferences](#social-preferences),
[Equity theory](#equity-theory) (Section \@ref(equity-theory)), [Psychological contract](#psychological-contract) (Section \@ref(psychological-contract)),
[Organizational justice](#organizational-justice) (Section \@ref(organizational-justice)), [Tournament theory](#tournament-theory) (Section \@ref(tournament-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Competitive theory predicts that wages fall until the labour market clears, so
persistent unemployment and firms' reluctance to cut pay in recessions are
puzzles. Efficiency wage theory resolves them by noting that the wage is also an
incentive. If productivity depends on the wage, a firm minimizes cost per
unit of effective labour, not cost per worker. With effort $e(w)$, the firm
chooses the wage that minimizes $w / e(w)$, which yields the condition that the
elasticity of effort with respect to the wage equals one [@solow1979]:

$$\frac{w\, e'(w)}{e(w)} \;=\; 1.$$

If this wage exceeds the market-clearing level, the firm will not lower it, and
unemployment persists.

Two micro-foundations dominate. In the **shirking model** of @shapiro1984,
shirkers are caught with probability $q$ and fired, a threat that bites only if
losing the job is costly. @akerlof1982, inspired by a study of clerical workers
who routinely exceeded their output standard, modelled employment as **partial
gift exchange**: the firm pays above the outside option, and workers reciprocate
with effort above the minimum. Other variants emphasize **turnover** costs and
**[adverse selection](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry))**.

### Core logic and propositions

In the shirking model, a worker prefers working to shirking when the wage
satisfies the **no-shirking condition** (NSC):

$$w \;\geq\; \bar{w} + e + \frac{e}{q}\left(r + \frac{b}{u}\right),$$

where $\bar{w}$ is the unemployment benefit, $e$ the disutility of effort, $q$
the detection probability, $r$ the discount rate, $b$ the exogenous separation
rate, and $u$ the unemployment rate. As unemployment falls, a fired worker finds
a new job quickly, so the wage needed to deter shirking rises without limit.
Full employment is incompatible with discipline: some unemployment is necessary
to make dismissal a credible threat. The family of models yields these
propositions:

- **P1 (Wage premium).** Firms pay above the market-clearing wage when effort,
  quality, or retention depends on the wage.
- **P2 (Monitoring substitution).** Wage premiums are higher where monitoring is
  costly or detection is unlikely.
- **P3 (Reciprocity).** Wage gifts perceived as generous relative to a reference
  wage elicit higher effort [@akerlof1982].
- **P4 (Involuntary unemployment).** Equilibrium unemployment persists even
  though unemployed workers would accept the going wage [@shapiro1984].
- **P5 (Wage rigidity).** Firms resist cutting wages in downturns because cuts
  damage morale and effort.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-nsc) plots the no-shirking condition against labour
demand. Equilibrium occurs where the curves cross, to the left of full
employment, and the gap is involuntary unemployment.

```{r fig-econ-nsc, fig.cap = "Stylised Shapiro-Stiglitz model. The no-shirking wage rises steeply as employment approaches the labour force, so equilibrium (where labour demand meets the no-shirking condition) leaves some workers involuntarily unemployed.", fig.height = 4.2}
N <- 100; e_cost <- 1; q_det <- 0.5; r_disc <- 0.05; b_sep <- 0.1; w_bar <- 0.5
nsc <- function(L) w_bar + e_cost + (e_cost / q_det) * (r_disc + b_sep * N / (N - L))
ld  <- function(L) 7 - 0.05 * L
L_star <- uniroot(function(L) nsc(L) - ld(L), c(1, 99))$root
emp <- seq(0, 97, by = 0.5)
curves <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(L = emp, w = nsc(emp), curve = "No-shirking condition"),
  data.frame(L = seq(0, 100, 0.5), w = ld(seq(0, 100, 0.5)), curve = "Labour demand")
)
ggplot(curves, aes(L, w, colour = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = N, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("point", x = L_star, y = ld(L_star), size = 3.2, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("segment", x = L_star, xend = N, y = 1.5, yend = 1.5, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.08, "inches"))) +
  annotate("text", x = (L_star + N) / 2, y = 0.8, label = "Involuntary\nunemployment",
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 101.2, y = 5, label = "Labour force", angle = 90, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("No-shirking condition" = pal[["orange"]], "Labour demand" = pal[["blue"]])) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 8), xlim = c(40, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Employment (labour force = 100)", y = "Real wage", colour = NULL,
       title = "Unemployment as a worker discipline device",
       caption = "Stylised parameters: e = 1, q = 0.5, r = 0.05, b = 0.1, unemployment benefit = 0.5.")
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-effwage) compares the main variants of the theory.

```{r tab-econ-effwage}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Variant, ~`Why higher wages raise productivity`, ~`Key prediction`, ~`Illustrative evidence`,
  "Shirking", "Job loss is costlier, so workers shirk less", "Premiums higher where monitoring is hard", "Cappelli & Chauvin (1991)",
  "Gift exchange", "Workers reciprocate generous pay with effort", "Effort rises with wage relative to reference", "Fehr, Kirchsteiger & Riedl (1993)",
  "Turnover", "Workers quit less, saving hiring and training costs", "Premiums higher where training is firm-specific", "Raff & Summers (1987)",
  "Adverse selection", "Higher wages attract a better applicant pool", "Applicant quality rises with posted wage", "Applicant pools at high-wage employers",
  "Morale and wage rigidity", "Pay cuts are seen as unfair and damage morale", "Firms prefer layoffs to pay cuts in downturns", "Bewley (1999)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Variants of efficiency wage theory.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

@raff1987 examined the Ford Motor Company's introduction of the five-dollar day
in 1914. After the change, turnover and absenteeism fell sharply, long queues
of applicants formed at the plant, and the authors found evidence of
productivity gains, a pattern they interpret as consistent with efficiency
wages rather than a simple response to a labour shortage. @krueger1988 documented large and persistent wage differences
across industries for observably similar workers, which are hard to reconcile
with competitive labour markets. @cappelli1991 found that plants paying larger
premiums over local wages had lower rates of disciplinary dismissal, as the
shirking model predicts.

In experimental labour markets, @fehr1993 found that employers offered wages
well above the market-clearing level and workers reciprocated with higher
effort. Interviewing managers, @bewley1999 concluded that firms avoid pay cuts
mainly to protect morale. In the field, @gneezy2006 found that an unexpectedly
high wage raised effort in the first hours of a short task, but the effect
faded quickly.

::: {.debate}
**Efficiency wages or something else?** Inter-industry wage differentials may
reflect unmeasured worker ability, compensating differentials for unpleasant
work, or rent sharing rather than efficiency wages. Deferred compensation and
seniority-based pay can in principle discipline workers without unemployment,
which raises the question of why firms rely on wage premiums. The decay of
gift-exchange effects in short field experiments [@gneezy2006] suggests that
reciprocity may be strongest in long-term relationships, precisely where it is
hardest to test cleanly.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Ford's five-dollar day and Costco's wage policy.** Ford's 1914 policy, which
roughly doubled pay for eligible workers, is the canonical efficiency wage case
[@raff1987]. A modern counterpart is the comparison between Costco and Walmart's
Sam's Club. @cascio2006 documented that Costco paid considerably higher wages
and benefits than its warehouse-club rival and argued that it was rewarded
with lower employee turnover and higher productivity. The logic is the one in
Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-effwage): the relevant cost is labour cost per unit of
effective output, and when turnover and service quality depend on pay, the
cheapest wage per worker can be the most expensive wage per unit of output.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Establishments that pay a larger premium over the local market wage will
  experience lower voluntary turnover and fewer disciplinary dismissals.
- *H2.* The effect of a wage increase on effort will be larger when the increase
  is framed as discretionary (a gift) than when it is mandated.

**Designs.** Natural experiments from minimum wage changes or firm-level wage
policy changes, linked employer-employee panels, field experiments with
temporary workers, laboratory gift-exchange games.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Assuming any wage increase pays for itself.** The theory says that the
cost-minimizing wage may exceed the market wage, not that higher wages always
raise profits. A premium that is not noticed, not attributed to the employer's
generosity, or matched by every competitor yields little extra effort.
:::

## Network Effects {#network-effects}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** When the value of a product to each user rises with the number
of other users, demand exhibits positive feedback. Markets can **tip** toward a
single product or standard, expectations about who will win become
self-fulfilling, and an inferior technology can become **locked in**.

**Origins.** Industrial organization. @katz1985, @farrell1985, @arthur1989, with
the historical case of the typewriter keyboard in @david1985.

**Level of analysis.** Market and industry.

**Key constructs.** Direct and indirect network effects, installed base,
expectations, compatibility, switching costs, tipping, lock-in, excess inertia.

**Boundary conditions.** Value depends substantially on network size,
multi-homing is costly, and products are not highly differentiated. Local
network effects and cheap multi-homing reduce tipping.

**Related theories.** [Two-sided markets](#two-sided-markets),
[Diffusion of innovations](#diffusion-of-innovations) (Section \@ref(diffusion-of-innovations)), [Dominant design](#dominant-design) (Section \@ref(dominant-design)),
[First-mover advantage](#first-mover-advantage) (Section \@ref(first-mover-advantage)), [Bass model](#bass-model) (Section \@ref(bass-model)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

**Direct network effects** arise when users benefit directly from others'
adoption (telephones, messaging). **Indirect network effects** arise when a
larger user base attracts more complementary products (consoles and games). @katz1985 modelled competition among firms whose products exhibit
network externalities and showed that consumer expectations about network size
determine equilibrium outcomes. @farrell1985 analysed the
coordination problem of switching to a new standard and identified **excess
inertia**, in which users stick with an old standard because no one wants to move
first, and its mirror image, excess momentum.

@arthur1989 placed these ideas in a broader frame. Under increasing returns to
adoption, the process of technology competition is path dependent: small
historical events early in the process can determine which technology wins, the
outcome is not predictable in advance, and the winner need not be the better
technology. @david1985 argued that the QWERTY keyboard layout was such a case.

### Core logic and propositions

A standard formulation gives consumer $i$ utility from product $k$ of

$$u_{ik} \;=\; r_{ik} + v\!\left(n_k^{e}\right) - p_k,$$

where $r_{ik}$ is stand-alone value, $n_k^{e}$ is the expected number of users,
and $v(\cdot)$ is increasing. Because utility depends on expectations about
others' choices, there can be multiple **fulfilled-expectations equilibria**:
if everyone expects product A to win, everyone adopts A, and the expectation is
confirmed. The theory implies:

- **P1 (Tipping).** With strong network effects and costly multi-homing, markets
  tend toward a single dominant product.
- **P2 (Expectations).** Firms that shape expectations about future network size
  (through announcements, alliances, or commitments) can win even with a smaller
  installed base [@katz1985].
- **P3 (Compatibility strategy).** Firms with large networks or strong
  reputations tend to oppose compatibility, while smaller firms favour it
  [@katz1985].
- **P4 (Path dependence and lock-in).** Early random events can decide the
  outcome, and an inferior standard can persist because switching requires
  coordination [@arthur1989; @farrell1985].
- **P5 (Limits).** Differentiation, local network effects, and cheap multi-homing
  reduce winner-take-all outcomes.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-tipping) simulates Arthur's argument. Two technologies
start with identical support, and each new adopter chooses technology A with a
probability that rises more than proportionally with A's current share. Chance
early choices decide the winner, and most runs drift toward dominance by one
technology.

```{r fig-econ-tipping, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of increasing returns to adoption. Each line is one market with identical starting conditions. Because each adopter favours the technology with the larger installed base, chance early choices tip markets toward one technology or the other.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1989)
simulate_market <- function(run, n_adopt = 1000, gamma = 1.6) {
  a <- 10; b <- 10; share <- numeric(n_adopt)        # identical installed bases at launch
  for (t in seq_len(n_adopt)) {
    s <- a / (a + b)
    p_a <- s^gamma / (s^gamma + (1 - s)^gamma)   # increasing returns: p_a > s when s > 0.5
    if (runif(1) < p_a) a <- a + 1 else b <- b + 1
    share[t] <- a / (a + b)
  }
  data.frame(run = run, adopter = seq_len(n_adopt), share = share)
}
runs <- bind_rows(lapply(1:14, simulate_market)) |>
  group_by(run) |>
  mutate(winner = if (last(share) > 0.5) "Technology A wins" else "Technology B wins") |>
  ungroup()
ggplot(runs, aes(adopter, share, group = run, colour = winner)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Technology A wins" = pal[["blue"]], "Technology B wins" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Number of adopters", y = "Installed-base share of technology A", colour = NULL,
       title = "Identical starts, divergent outcomes",
       caption = "Illustrative simulation: P(choose A) = s^1.6 / (s^1.6 + (1 - s)^1.6), s = A's current share. Both start with 10 users.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

@katz1994 review evidence and theory on systems competition. Empirically,
estimating network effects is difficult because users who are connected tend to
be similar and are exposed to common shocks. @tucker2008 used variation in the
adoption of a video-messaging technology within an investment bank to separate
network effects from correlated behaviour, and found that how much a colleague's
adoption mattered depended on that colleague's position in the formal hierarchy
and the informal communication network.

The lock-in claim has been contested. @liebowitz1990 re-examined the QWERTY case
and argued that the evidence for the superiority of the rival Dvorak layout was
weak and that markets had not demonstrably locked in an inferior standard. Their
critique shifted the burden of proof: documenting path dependence is not the
same as documenting inefficient lock-in.

```{r tab-econ-network}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Strategy, ~`Network-effects logic`, ~Example, ~Risk,
  "Penetration pricing", "Subsidize early adopters to build the installed base", "Free tiers for consumer software", "Customers anchor on a low price",
  "Seeding and targeting hubs", "Win central users whose adoption influences others", "Launching in a dense community first", "Hubs may multi-home",
  "Compatibility and adapters", "Borrow a rival's network", "Backward-compatible consoles, file-format import", "Strengthens the rival standard",
  "Open standard or licensing", "Grow the whole network quickly", "Broad licensing of a format to manufacturers", "Lose control of rents",
  "Expectation management", "Make adoption look inevitable", "Preannouncements, alliance announcements", "Credibility loss if late",
  "Lock-in through switching costs", "Make exit costly once users join", "Proprietary data formats, loyalty programmes", "Antitrust and customer resentment"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Competitive strategies in markets with network effects.")
```

::: {.debate}
**How strong are network effects in practice?** Strategy writing often treats
network effects as an impregnable moat. History suggests caution: dominant social
networks have been displaced, and many networked markets support several
competitors. Researchers increasingly distinguish the *strength* of network
effects, their *scope* (global versus local), and the *cost of multi-homing*,
each of which moderates the tipping prediction.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**VHS versus Betamax.** Sony introduced the Betamax videocassette format in 1975
and JVC introduced VHS in 1976. The formats were incompatible, and the value of a
recorder depended on the availability of pre-recorded tapes, an indirect network
effect. JVC licensed VHS widely to other manufacturers, and early VHS machines
offered longer recording times. As the VHS installed base grew, video rental
stores stocked more VHS titles, which further increased VHS's advantage. By the
late 1980s VHS dominated, and Sony began producing VHS recorders in 1988. The
case illustrates tipping and the strategic value of licensing to build an
installed base (Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-network)). Whether Betamax was
technically superior matters less to the theory than how an early lead in
complements became decisive.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The effect of installed base on a product's market share will be larger
  in categories with higher multi-homing costs.
- *H2.* Product preannouncements will slow adoption of a rival standard more in
  markets with strong indirect network effects.

**Designs.** Demand estimation with installed-base terms and instruments,
peer-effects designs exploiting exogenous variation in network exposure,
historical case comparisons of standards battles, agent-based simulation.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Confusing popularity with network effects.** Network effects require that each
user's value depends on others' use. Popularity driven by quality, advertising,
or social learning produces similar adoption curves but different strategic
implications. Identify the mechanism before invoking tipping.
:::

## Two-Sided Markets {#two-sided-markets}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** A platform that serves two distinct groups linked by **cross-side
[network effects](#network-effects)** chooses not only a price level but a **price structure**. It
typically subsidizes the side whose participation creates more value for the
other side and whose demand is more price-sensitive, and earns its margin on the
other side.

**Origins.** Industrial organization. @rochet2003, @caillaud2003,
@parker2005, @armstrong2006, reviewed in @rochet2006 and @rysman2009.

**Level of analysis.** Platform and market.

**Key constructs.** Cross-side externality, price level versus price structure,
subsidy side and money side, multi-homing, competitive bottleneck,
chicken-and-egg problem.

**Boundary conditions.** A market is two-sided when the volume of transactions
depends on how the total price is split between the sides, not only on its
level. If the sides can pass charges through to each other, the market is
effectively one-sided.

**Related theories.** [Network effects](#network-effects),
[Transaction cost economics](#transaction-cost-economics) (Section \@ref(transaction-cost-economics)),
[Competitive dynamics](#competitive-dynamics) (Section \@ref(competitive-dynamics)), [Resource dependence theory](#resource-dependence-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-dependence-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Many networked businesses connect two groups that value each other: cardholders
and merchants, players and game developers, riders and drivers. @rochet2003 showed that in such markets, the allocation of
charges across sides matters, and that the profit-maximizing structure can
involve prices below marginal cost on one side. @parker2005 reached a similar
conclusion from information-product design: Adobe could give away its Acrobat
Reader to consumers because doing so raised the value of its paid authoring
software to document creators. @caillaud2003 analysed the chicken-and-egg
problem of attracting both sides at once and the "divide-and-conquer" strategy of
subsidizing one side to attract the other.

### Core logic and propositions

@rochet2006 offer a precise definition. Let a platform charge $a^{B}$ per
transaction to buyers and $a^{S}$ to sellers. The market is two-sided if the
volume of transactions depends on $a^{B}$ and $a^{S}$ separately and not only on
their sum $a^{B} + a^{S}$. In @armstrong2006's model of a monopoly platform, the
utility of a group-1 member is $u_1 = \alpha_1 n_2 - p_1$, where $\alpha_1$ is
the benefit from each member of group 2, and participation is $n_1 = \phi_1(u_1)$.
The profit-maximizing price for group 1 is

$$p_1 \;=\; f_1 \;-\; \alpha_2 n_2 \;+\; \frac{\phi_1(u_1)}{\phi_1'(u_1)},$$

where $f_1$ is the cost of serving a group-1 member. The middle term is the key
insight: the price to group 1 is lowered by the external benefit an additional
member confers on group 2, and can be zero or negative. The theory implies:

- **P1 (Price structure).** The side that generates larger cross-side benefits and
  has more elastic demand receives lower prices, possibly below cost.
- **P2 (Skewed pricing is not predation).** A below-cost price on one side is
  consistent with profit maximization and does not by itself indicate
  anticompetitive intent [@rochet2006].
- **P3 (Competitive bottlenecks).** When one side multi-homes and the other
  single-homes, platforms compete for the single-homing side and charge the
  multi-homing side for access to it [@armstrong2006].
- **P4 (Chicken and egg).** Platforms must solve a coordination problem at launch,
  often by subsidizing or seeding one side [@caillaud2003].

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-platform) shows the feedback loop that the price
structure manages.

```{r fig-econ-platform, fig.cap = "Mechanism of a two-sided platform: the price charged to each side determines its participation, and each side's participation raises the value of the platform to the other side. The platform chooses which side to subsidize."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  PA [label = "Price to side A\\n(e.g., consumers)", %s]
  PB [label = "Price to side B\\n(e.g., developers)", %s]
  NA [label = "Participation\\nof side A", %s]
  NB [label = "Participation\\nof side B", %s]
  R  [label = "Platform profit", %s]
  M  [label = "Multi-homing\\ncosts", %s]
  PA -> NA
  PB -> NB
  NA -> NB [label = " cross-side\\n value"]
  NB -> NA [label = " cross-side\\n value"]
  NA -> R
  NB -> R
  M -> NB [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-platforms) gives examples of price structures.

```{r tab-econ-platforms}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Platform, ~`Side A`, ~`Side B`, ~`Typical price structure`,
  "Payment cards", "Cardholders", "Merchants", "Cardholders often pay little or receive rewards. Merchants pay fees per transaction",
  "App stores", "Device users", "App developers", "Many apps free to download. Developers pay commissions on paid apps and in-app purchases",
  "Ride-hailing", "Riders", "Drivers", "Both sides priced, with dynamic prices balancing supply and demand",
  "Video game consoles", "Players", "Game publishers", "Hardware has often been sold near cost. Publishers pay royalties",
  "Search and social media", "Users", "Advertisers", "Users pay nothing. Advertisers pay for attention",
  "Document formats", "Readers", "Authors", "Free reader software. Paid authoring software (Parker & Van Alstyne, 2005)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Price structures on two-sided platforms.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

Payment cards are the most studied case. Interchange fees, paid by the
merchant's bank to the cardholder's bank, shift costs between the sides, and
regulators have capped them: the European Union's 2015 Interchange Fee
Regulation capped consumer debit and credit interchange at 0.2 and 0.3 percent of
transaction value, and in the United States the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act (through the
Durbin Amendment) capped debit interchange for large issuers. Two-sidedness also
reached the United States Supreme Court: in *Ohio v. American Express* (2018),
the Court held that the credit-card market must be analysed as two-sided,
weighing effects on both merchants and cardholders. @rysman2009 reviews the
broader empirical literature.

::: {.debate}
**Efficient structure or market power?** Two-sided theory explains why a platform
might charge one side heavily without implying abuse. Critics worry that the
theory can be used to excuse high charges to a side that has no alternative, for
instance merchants who cannot refuse a popular card or developers who cannot
reach users except through a dominant app store. The analytical challenge is to
separate the *structure* of prices, which may be legitimately skewed, from their
*level*, which can reflect market power. A second debate concerns definitions:
almost every firm intermediates between some groups, so two-sided analysis
requires showing that cross-side effects are material.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**App store commissions.** Apple's App Store has long charged developers a
standard commission of 30 percent on paid apps and in-app purchases of digital
goods, while letting users download free apps at no charge. Two-sided theory
explains the structure: users single-home on a phone platform and are the side
developers need to reach, so the platform subsidizes users and charges the side
that multi-homes (a competitive bottleneck). The structure has been contested.
In 2021 Apple introduced a Small Business Program that cut the commission to 15
percent for developers with up to one million dollars in annual proceeds, and
litigation such as *Epic Games v. Apple* and the European Union's Digital
Markets Act have targeted its payment and distribution rules. A price structure
that maximizes short-run profit can provoke the regulatory and competitive
responses that reshape it. Ride-hailing shows a different case:
because drivers multi-home across apps and riders compare fares, both sides are
price-sensitive, and dynamic pricing must balance them continuously, subject to
the fairness limits discussed under [Social preferences](#social-preferences).
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Platforms will charge lower prices to the side whose participation
  generates stronger cross-side effects.
- *H2.* Regulatory caps on fees to one side will be partly offset by higher fees
  or lower subsidies on the other side (a "waterbed" effect).

**Designs.** Structural demand models with cross-side effects,
difference-in-differences around fee regulation, natural experiments in platform entry, field
experiments that vary fees to one side.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Applying one-sided price-cost tests.** Concluding that a zero price to users
is predatory, or that a high fee to merchants is exploitative, by looking at
one side alone ignores the cross-side externality. Analyse total price and
total cost across both sides before drawing conclusions about efficiency or
competition.
:::

## Auction Theory {#auction-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** The rules of a sale (who bids, in what format, with what
information and reserve price) determine bidding strategies, revenue, and
whether the good goes to the bidder who values it most. Under benchmark
assumptions many formats yield the same expected revenue, but departures from
those assumptions, especially common values, asymmetric bidders, collusion, and
entry costs, make design decisive.

**Origins.** Economics and game theory. @vickrey1961, @myerson1981,
@riley1981, and @milgrom1982. Vickrey shared the 1996 Nobel Memorial Prize, and
Milgrom and Robert Wilson received the 2020 prize.

**Level of analysis.** Market mechanism, bidder, and seller.

**Key constructs.** Private versus common values, bid shading, dominant strategy,
revenue equivalence, reserve price, winner's curse, affiliation, linkage
principle, collusion, entry.

**Boundary conditions.** The benchmark results assume risk-neutral bidders with
independent private values from a common distribution, no collusion, and a
fixed number of bidders.

**Related theories.** [Game theory](#game-theory) (Section \@ref(game-theory)),
[Information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry)), [Search theory](#search-theory),
[Social preferences](#social-preferences).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@vickrey1961 founded the field by analysing auctions as games of incomplete
information. He showed that when the highest bidder pays the *second*-highest
bid, bidding one's true value is a dominant strategy. He also anticipated the
**revenue equivalence theorem**, generalized by @myerson1981 and @riley1981:
with risk-neutral bidders and independent private values, any auction that
gives the good to the highest bidder and zero surplus to a bidder with the
lowest possible value yields the same expected revenue.

@milgrom1982 extended the analysis to settings in which bidders' values are
**affiliated**, as when the value of an oil tract depends partly on the unknown
amount of oil, which all bidders estimate with noise. In such settings the
English auction yields expected revenue at least as high as the second-price
auction, which in turn yields at least as much as the first-price auction, and
sellers gain by committing to reveal information they hold (the **linkage
principle**). Petroleum engineers had already noticed a practical counterpart:
@capen1971 argued that
oil companies bidding for Gulf of Mexico leases earned disappointing returns
because the winner of a common-value auction is the bidder who most
overestimated the tract's value, the **winner's curse**.

### Core logic and propositions

With $n$ bidders whose private values are independent and uniformly distributed
on $[0, 1]$, the equilibrium strategies are:

$$b^{\text{2nd}}(v) = v, \qquad b^{\text{1st}}(v) = \frac{n-1}{n}\, v.$$

In the second-price auction, bidders bid their values. In the first-price
auction, they shade their bids, but the winner's expected payment in both cases
equals the expected second-highest value, $(n-1)/(n+1)$. In a common-value
auction where the item is worth $V$ to everyone and bidder $i$ observes a noisy
signal $s_i$, winning is bad news:

$$\mathbb{E}\left[V \mid s_i,\; s_i = \max_j s_j\right] \;<\; \mathbb{E}\left[V \mid s_i\right],$$

so a rational bidder must shade more as the number of competitors grows.
Table \@ref(tab:tab-econ-auctions) summarizes common formats. The propositions
are:

- **P1 (Truthful bidding).** In second-price and English auctions with private
  values, bidding one's value is a (weakly) dominant strategy [@vickrey1961].
- **P2 (Revenue equivalence).** Under the benchmark assumptions, standard formats
  yield equal expected revenue [@myerson1981; @riley1981].
- **P3 (Linkage principle).** With affiliated values, formats that link the price
  to more information, and sellers who disclose information, raise expected
  revenue [@milgrom1982].
- **P4 (Winner's curse).** In common-value auctions, naive bidders who bid their
  estimates lose money on average, and the loss grows with the number of bidders
  [@capen1971; @thaler1988].
- **P5 (Design for entry and against collusion).** In practice, attracting
  bidders and preventing collusion matter more than the fine points of the
  benchmark ranking [@klemperer2002].

```{r tab-econ-auctions}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Format, ~Rules, ~`Equilibrium bidding (private values)`, ~`Typical uses`,
  "English (ascending)", "Price rises until one bidder remains. Winner pays the final price", "Stay in until price reaches own value", "Art, real estate, livestock, online consumer auctions",
  "Dutch (descending)", "Price falls until a bidder accepts", "Strategically equivalent to first-price sealed bid", "Flowers, fish, perishable goods",
  "First-price sealed bid", "Highest bid wins and pays own bid", "Shade bid below value", "Public procurement, construction tenders",
  "Second-price sealed bid (Vickrey)", "Highest bid wins and pays second-highest bid", "Bid true value (dominant strategy)", "Benchmark in theory, some online ad systems",
  "Generalized second price", "Several ranked slots. Each winner pays the next bid", "Not truthful in general", "Sponsored search advertising",
  "Simultaneous ascending or clock auction", "Many items auctioned together over rounds", "Bid on items or packages as prices rise", "Spectrum licences, electricity, emission allowances"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Common auction formats.")
```

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-econ-winners) simulates the winner's curse. Each bidder
naively bids an unbiased but noisy estimate of a common value. The winning bid
is the highest estimate, which is biased upward, increasingly so as bidders are
added.

```{r fig-econ-winners, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of the winner's curse. A tract is worth 100 to every bidder. Each bidder receives an unbiased estimate with noise (standard deviation 15) and bids it. The winner's expected overpayment rises with the number of bidders. The band shows the 10th to 90th percentile across simulated auctions.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1971)
true_value <- 100
wc <- lapply(2:20, function(n) {
  win <- replicate(4000, max(true_value + rnorm(n, 0, 15)))   # naive bid = own estimate
  data.frame(n = n, mean = mean(win - true_value),
             lo = quantile(win - true_value, 0.1), hi = quantile(win - true_value, 0.9))
}) |> bind_rows()
ggplot(wc, aes(n, mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = pal[["blue"]], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["blue"]], size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 20, y = -6, label = "Zero line: winner pays the true value", hjust = 1,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 20, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Number of bidders", y = "Winning bid minus true value",
       title = "The more bidders, the worse the winner's curse for naive bidders",
       caption = "Illustrative: common value = 100, estimate noise ~ Normal(0, 15), 4,000 auctions per point.")
```

### Evidence and extensions
